metaTitle: Best Large Immersion Blenders for Big Pots 2026
metaDescription: Long-shaft stick blenders for stockpots, canning batches and big soup runs compared on shaft length, motor, lock mode and weight across six models.
expertTake: The VEVOR 750W 20 inch is the top pick for big home and small-catering batches, because it adds reach and a 750W copper motor at a mid-range price tier. The VONCI 500W 16 inch is the value pick, since a sealed SUS 304 shaft and a hands-free lock cost little. Skip the category if your biggest pot is a normal 6 quart stockpot, because a regular 8 inch stick is lighter and easier to handle.
introParagraphs: A large immersion blender is defined by its shaft. When the pot is deep and the batch is big, whether it is tomato sauce for canning, soup for a crowd or stock for a catering order, a standard 8 inch stick cannot reach the bottom and forces you to tilt a heavy pot.

Reach brings its own problems: a long shaft is hard to balance, a bigger motor runs hotter, and the tool is awkward to wash and store. This guide compares long-shaft sticks on how they balance reach against weight, how they run for long sessions and how they come apart for cleaning.

products.name: VEVOR 750W 20 inch heavy-duty immersion blender
products.description:
The 20 inch VEVOR is the strongest case for a large stick at a sensible price. A 750 watt pure copper motor drives a 20 inch stainless shaft, which clears the bottom of a deep 40 quart stockpot with a hand's width to spare. A rubberized grip and a detachable assembly keep it usable, and variable speed lets you start slowly.

The length is what you are paying for. At 20 inches you can blend a full canning pot of tomato sauce without tilting it, which is safer with a boiling vessel. A detachable design lets you rotate the shaft off the motor for cleaning, so a sticky puree never reaches the housing.

Expect a long tool. The overall length means you need a tall rack or a hook for storage, and the weight is felt at the end of a long run. Rest the motor on the pot rim between passes and keep the shaft vertical. Rinse it immediately and check the detachable joint for wear. It is the best-balanced of the long sticks here.
products.bestFor: Big home batches and small-catering pots up to about 40 quarts.
pros: Variable speed for a gentle start
cons: Long overall length is awkward to store
Heavy at the end of a long run

products.name: VEVOR 750W 16 inch heavy-duty variable-speed hand mixer
products.description:
The 16 inch VEVOR uses the same 750 watt copper motor as its 20 inch sibling on a shorter shaft. The listing specifies 304 stainless steel and a detachable design with variable speed. It is lighter at the end of the arm than the 20 inch model, which makes it the easier of the two to hold for a long time.

Sixteen inches reaches the floor of a 20 to 30 quart pot, which covers most home-scale batch cooking. The motor is the same, so the choice between this and the 20 inch is purely about pot depth. If your deepest pot is under about 14 inches, this is the better balanced tool.

It is also cheaper by a small step in price tier. Clean it the way you would the 20 inch: rotate off the shaft, rinse the foot and dry the joint before storage. Check the stainless for dents, since a bent shaft wobbles under load. It suits cooks who want power without the longest reach.
products.bestFor: Cooks with 20 to 30 quart pots who want power without extra length.
pros: 750W copper motor on a lighter 16 inch shaft
cons: Does not reach the floor of very deep kettles
Overall length still needs a hook for storage

products.name: VONCI 500W 16 inch commercial immersion blender, SUS 304 shaft
products.description:
The VONCI is the budget long stick. A 500 watt pure copper motor drives a 16 inch sealed SUS 304 shaft, with an anti-splash blade and variable speed. The feature that sets it apart in this group is a hands-free lock mode, which keeps the motor running without squeezing a trigger.

On a big batch the lock mode matters more than the wattage. When you are standing at a stockpot for ten minutes, a held switch tires the hand, and a lock lets you steer the shaft with both hands. A sealed SUS 304 shaft is also easier to keep clean than a joint with exposed threads.

At 500 watts it is lighter on power than the 750 watt VEVORs, so it is better for soups and sauces than for thick purees. Keep the batch size sensible and rest between runs. Wash the shaft after each use and check the seal for pits. It is the pick for cooks who want a long reach on a tight budget.
products.bestFor: Cooks who blend big pots of soup and sauce and want a hands-free lock.
pros: Hands-free lock mode for long runs
Lowest price tier of the long sticks
cons: 500W trails the 750W models on thick food
Lock mode needs care around hot liquids

products.name: VEVOR 500W 16 inch heavy-duty mixer, stepless 4,000 to 16,000 rpm
products.description:
This VEVOR 500 watt model swaps preset speeds for a stepless knob that runs from 4,000 to 16,000 rpm. The listing is careful to say that 16 inches is the shaft length and that the overall length is 30 inches, which is a useful reminder of how big these tools are.

A stepless knob is the best control for a big pot. You can crawl at 4,000 rpm while the head is still half-submerged and then climb to 16,000 as the vortex forms. That avoids the geyser that a fixed fast speed throws in a deep vessel. It sits between the 750 watt VEVOR and the cheaper VONCI in price tier.

The overall length means a tall store and a steady stance. Rest your forearm on the pot rim and keep the shaft vertical. Rinse it right away and dry the joint. Cooks who value speed control over a bigger motor will find the stepless knob the main draw.
products.bestFor: Cooks who want a stepless knob on a long shaft.
cons: 30 inch overall length is awkward to store

products.name: Subry Chefy 1000W 25-speed stainless corded immersion blender
products.description:
The Subry Chefy is a home-size stick that earns a place by being the lightest. A 1000 watt headline brushless copper motor, a stainless body and a crafted handle designed to be comfortable make it easy to hold for a long soup. Twenty-five speed settings give the finest dial in this guide.

It is large only in the sense of capacity, not length. The listing does not publish a long shaft, so treat it as a big-batch tool for a normal deep saucepan or a 6 to 8 quart pot. The brushless motor is meant to deliver steady power and a longer working life than a brushed motor.

The 1000 watt figure is a headline, so rely on the dial. Start at the lowest of the twenty-five steps and move up as the food softens. Wash the shaft after use and wipe the handle. It suits cooks who want a lighter stick for a bigger pot and do not need a very long shaft.
products.bestFor: Cooks with 6 to 8 quart pots who want the lightest stick.
cons: Shaft length is not stated as long

products.name: Robot Coupe MP 450 Turbo 18 inch fixed-speed power mixer
products.description:
The MP 450 Turbo is the benchmark for what a large stick can be. An 18 inch stainless shaft, a fixed speed and a stated capacity of 25 gallons, about 100 quarts, make it a professional tool. The listing stresses consistent performance on repetitive tasks and deep batches.

It is the heaviest-duty option in this guide and the only one built for a full shift in a commercial kitchen. A fixed speed means no dial, and nothing electronic to fail. The cost is flexibility: there is no gentle start, so you submerge the head fully before you press.

For a home cook it is overkill, but for a caterer or a food business it is the one that lasts. Remove the bell and shaft for cleaning, keep spare blades on the shelf and hang the unit by its handle. Compare it against the VEVOR 20 inch before you decide how much durability you need.
products.bestFor: Caterers and food businesses that blend big batches daily.
pros: Fixed speed with no dial to fail
cons: Fixed speed with no gentle start
Highest price tier and overkill at home

buyingCriteria.criterion: Shaft length for your deepest pot
buyingCriteria.explanation: A 16 inch shaft, as on the VEVOR 750W and VONCI, reaches the floor of a 20 to 30 quart pot. The VEVOR 20 inch clears a 40 quart stockpot, and the Robot Coupe MP 450 Turbo at 18 inches suits deep commercial pots. Measure the pot from rim to floor before you choose, and add an inch of margin. The classic error is buying by the maximum gallon figure and ignoring depth, which leaves the blade hovering above the floor of a tall, narrow pot.
The VEVOR 750W models and the Robot Coupe have the reserve for thick sauces. The 500W VEVOR and VONCI suit soups. The Subry Chefy quotes a 1000W headline, so judge by the dial and build.

A long shaft multiplies the weight at your wrist. The Subry Chefy is the lightest, the 20 inch VEVOR the longest. Rest the motor on the pot rim and keep the shaft vertical. Hold the stick with both hands when the pot is full, one on the grip and one on the shaft, because a long lever makes small wobbles into big splashes.

The VONCI has a hands-free lock mode for long runs. Others use a held switch. A lock saves the hand but needs care with hot liquid. If the lock is engaged you cannot rely on releasing a trigger to stop, so learn where the off switch is before you start, and keep the head submerged until the motor has fully stopped.

The 500W VEVOR offers a stepless knob from 4,000 to 16,000 rpm, the Subry Chefy twenty-five steps and the Robot Coupe a single speed. A slow start prevents geysers in deep pots. Choose the style you can control.

Detachable shafts, as on the VEVORs, rinse easily. A 30 inch overall length needs a hook or a tall rack. Plan where it will live before you buy. A stick that has to be unpacked from a high shelf every time ends up unused, and one that hangs by the stove gets reached for.

specDecoder.meaning: The shaft is the immersible part, while the overall length includes the motor. The overall figure tells you where it will fit.
specDecoder.watchFor: The 500W VEVOR lists a 16 inch shaft and a 30 inch overall length.

specDecoder.meaning: A food-grade stainless steel grade. It resists corrosion in acidic sauces.
specDecoder.watchFor: The VONCI lists a sealed SUS 304 shaft.

specDecoder.meaning: A motor without carbon brushes. It runs more efficiently and wears more slowly.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Subry Chefy lists a brushless copper motor.

specDecoder.meaning: A knob that runs through the whole range without fixed steps. It lets you set a very slow speed.
specDecoder.watchFor: The 500W VEVOR runs from 4,000 to 16,000 rpm.

specDecoder.meaning: A mode that keeps the motor running without a held switch. It reduces hand fatigue.

howWeEvaluated.title: Reach and pot fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared shaft lengths from 16 to 20 inches against typical pot depths. The VEVOR 20 inch leads for deep pots. Fit decides usefulness, so a stick that cannot reach the floor was ranked below one that can, whatever its other merits. We also noted the overall length, since a 30 inch tool is a storage decision as well as a cooking one.

howWeEvaluated.title: Motor reserve
howWeEvaluated.description: We read the ratings, from 500W to 750W and the 1000W headline. We weighted rated figures. Owner feedback patterns on heat in long runs informed the ranking.

howWeEvaluated.title: Handling over a long run
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered weight, lock mode and handle design. A lock saves the hand, a light body saves the wrist. The VONCI and Subry Chefy lead.

howWeEvaluated.title: Speed control
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stepless, stepped and fixed control. A slow start is vital in a deep pot. The stepless VEVOR leads.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value and durability
howWeEvaluated.description: We ordered the six by relative price tier, with the VONCI lowest and the Robot Coupe highest. Each step should buy reach, control or durability.

rows: Sealed shaft and a lock mode

cards.label: 750W
cards.text: The VEVOR 750W models and the Robot Coupe have reserve for thick purees and long runs.

cards.text: A shaft that reaches the floor of a hot pot without tilting, a lock mode or a comfortable grip and a stainless shaft. Boiling sauce demands care.

maintenance.why: Tomato and soup solids dry quickly. A rinse prevents staining.
A damp joint corrodes over time. Rotate the shaft off and let it dry.
A pitted seal lets liquid into the shaft. Replace the shaft if it leaks.
Long runs heat the motor. A pause protects the windings.
A long shaft bends if it leans. A hook keeps it straight. A wall-mounted hook at head height also keeps the cord off the floor and the motor away from damp counters.

faq.q: What makes an immersion blender large?
faq.a: A long shaft and a motor built for big batches. Most large sticks run 16 to 22 inches. Check whether the figure quoted is the shaft or the overall length, since the two differ by a foot or more and the overall number decides where the stick will fit.

faq.q: Do I need a large stick at home?
faq.a: Only for deep pots or big batches. A regular stick is easier to handle for normal cooking. If your biggest job is a 6 quart pot of soup once a month, a long stick will spend most of its life on a hook, so buy length only for the pot you really use.

For soups and sauces, yes. Thick purees favour 750W. A 500W stick will still manage a big pot of tomato sauce, but it runs warmer and takes longer, so rest it between passes and do not push it through a dry paste.

faq.q: How do I blend hot sauce safely?
faq.a: Submerge the head before starting and keep the shaft vertical. Let it cool slightly first. Never tilt a pot of boiling sauce to reach the blade, and never lift the head out while the motor is running, because the spray from a deep pot is serious.

faq.q: How do I store a long stick?
faq.a: Hang it on a hook or keep it in a tall rack. Leaning bends the shaft.

faq.q: Are commercial sticks worth it at home?
faq.a: Only if you cook very large batches. They are heavy and expensive. The Robot Coupe is built for a shift of repeated starts, which a home cook will never use, so the extra cost buys durability that stays theoretical.
